question: HDD latency
points: Rotational latency is the delay while the required disk sector rotates under the read/write head.

question: Network interface card (NIC)

chapterName: Networks and the effects of using them
title: MAC addresses: purpose and format
question: MAC addresses: purpose and format
points: MAC stands for Media Access Control.
A MAC address identifies a network interface on a local network.
A typical MAC address is 48 bits long, written as six pairs of hexadecimal digits.
For a manufacturer-assigned address, the first part identifies the manufacturer and the remaining part identifies the interface.
A switch uses destination MAC addresses to forward data to the appropriate port.
Replacing the network interface changes its manufacturer-assigned MAC address.
advice: Use MAC addressing for local switching and IP addressing for routing between networks.

chapterName: Networks and the effects of using them
title: IPv4 versus IPv6
question: IPv4 versus IPv6
points: IPv4 addresses are 32 bits long.
IPv4 is normally written as four decimal numbers separated by full stops, for example 192.168.1.10.
IPv6 addresses are 128 bits long.
IPv6 is normally written in hexadecimal groups separated by colons.
IPv6 provides a much larger address space to support more connected devices.
Both versions identify network locations and support routing of packets.
textbookScope: 32-bit dotted decimal versus 128-bit hexadecimal addressing; address-space expansion.
sourceBasis: Generic topic recall synthesised from mapped Cambridge evidence and supplied textbook; contextual wording adapted. Model-specific limits and projected benefits are qualified.

chapterName: Networks and the effects of using them
title: MAC versus IP addresses
question: MAC versus IP addresses
points: A MAC address identifies a network interface; an IP address identifies its logical network location.
A typical MAC address is 48 bits; IPv4 uses 32 bits and IPv6 uses 128 bits.
MAC addresses are normally written in hexadecimal; IPv4 uses dotted decimal.
A manufacturer-assigned MAC normally remains with the interface; an IP address can change between networks.
Switches use MAC addresses for local forwarding; routers use IP addresses to route between networks.
textbookScope: Physical interface identifier versus logical network address; textbook discussion of persistence and location.

title: Data packets and packet headers
question: Data packets and packet headers
points: A message can be divided into smaller units called data packets.
Each packet carries part of the data and addressing or control information.
The textbook packet model includes source and destination IP addresses.
Sequence numbers allow the receiving system to put the data back in order.
Packet length and information about the complete message help the receiving system check reconstruction.
The destination address is used to forward a packet towards its destination.

title: Hubs: operation and limitations
question: Hubs: operation and limitations
points: A hub connects multiple devices to form or extend a LAN.
It repeats incoming signals to the other connected devices.
It does not select a destination by looking up a MAC address.
All connected devices receive the transmitted data even when it is intended for one device.
This creates unnecessary traffic and shares the available bandwidth.
Sending data to all devices makes interception easier than with targeted switch forwarding.

question: Hubs versus switches
points: Both connect devices together to form a LAN.

question: Network security: chapter scope
points: Hacking is gaining unauthorised access to a computer system.

chapterName: Networks and the effects of using them
title: Passwords and user IDs: purpose
question: Passwords and user IDs: purpose
points: A user ID identifies the account the user wants to access.
A password is a secret used to authenticate the person accessing that account.
Knowing a user ID alone should not give access without the required authentication.
Accounts can have different permissions or access levels.
User IDs allow administrators to monitor account activity.
Repeated incorrect login attempts may cause temporary account lockout.
Masking passwords reduces casual viewing during entry.
advice: The user ID identifies the account; the password authenticates access. Do not assume all passwords are unique.

points: A controller can adjust operation according to sensor readings or a selected programme.
Automatic shut-off can avoid leaving a device running unnecessarily.
Heating can be timed or remotely adjusted so energy is used when needed.
Appropriate control can reduce utility bills.
Stored programmes reduce the need to enter every setting manually.
Some appliances can read coded instructions to select suitable settings.
Energy savings depend on the device and how it is used.

question: Waste, complexity and standby energy use
points: Complex electronics can make repairs expensive.
Replacing failed devices can increase electronic waste.
Unfamiliar controls can be difficult for less-confident users.
Users may need time or training to learn the interface.
Standby and network functions can continue consuming electricity.
Dependence on automatic devices can make breakdowns disruptive.
The purchase and maintenance costs may outweigh savings for some users.

title: Connected home devices: data-security risks
question: Connected home devices: data-security risks
points: Connected home devices can provide a route for unauthorised remote access.
Default, weak or missing passwords make access easier to compromise.
An attacker may view camera footage or obtain private household information.
Remote access can expose information about when the home is unoccupied.
Stored account or payment details may be disclosed.
An attacker may change settings or disrupt operation.
Security risks arise from network access as well as the physical appliance.

points: Replace default passwords with strong, hard-to-guess passwords.
Use different passwords for different accounts or devices where supported.
Keep device software and security updates current.
Restrict access to authorised users.
Protect the home network with appropriate authentication and encryption.
Avoid exposing private information or access credentials.
Review available security settings when setting up connected devices.

question: Social interaction: positive effects
points: Labour-saving devices can free time for meeting friends and family.
Online communication helps people keep in touch over long distances.
VoIP, email and messaging allow convenient communication from home.
Online groups help people find others with shared interests.
Information and ideas can be shared with several people at once.
People unable to travel can participate in social or group activities.

question: Social interaction: negative effects
points: Heavy use of digital communication can reduce face-to-face interaction.

title: Transport monitoring/control applications
question: Transport monitoring/control applications
points: Computers monitor and control transport using sensors, processing and output devices.
Traffic-monitoring systems collect information about congestion and incidents.
Traffic lights can be adjusted to control vehicle flow.
ANPR identifies vehicle registration numbers from camera images.
Air-traffic and railway systems coordinate movements and schedules.
Sensors provide input; the processor makes decisions; signals or actuators produce outputs.
Monitoring gathers information, while control changes what happens.
advice: Distinguish the sensor, processor and actuator roles; explain monitoring separately from control.

title: ANPR: enforcement and privacy
question: ANPR: enforcement and privacy
points: ANPR stands for Automatic Number Plate Recognition.
A camera captures an image and software isolates the number plate.
OCR converts the plate's characters into machine-readable data.
The registration is compared with database records.
A match can identify an authorised vehicle, an offence or a vehicle of interest, depending on the system.
Records of location and time can track people's movements.
Unauthorised access or misuse of the database can invade privacy.
Dirty or obscured plates can cause recognition errors.
textbookScope: Detect offences, stolen vehicles and criminals; risk of tracking innocent people's movements and misuse of access.

title: Autonomous vehicles: meaning and public acceptance
question: Autonomous vehicles: meaning and public acceptance
points: An autonomous vehicle uses computer systems to perform driving tasks without a human carrying out those tasks.
Sensors gather information about the environment.
Software processes the information and decides how the vehicle should respond.
Actuators carry out actions such as steering or braking.
Public acceptance depends on trust in safety, reliability and security.
Driverless trains operate on constrained routes, while road vehicles face more varied surroundings.
The required human involvement depends on the vehicle's level and conditions of automation.
textbookScope: Driverless vehicles, perceived risks, trust and comparison with fixed-track autonomous trains.
sourceBasis: Generic topic recall synthesised from mapped Cambridge evidence and supplied textbook; contextual wording adapted. Model-specific limits and projected benefits are qualified.

title: Autonomous road vehicles: components
question: Autonomous road vehicles: components
points: Sensors measure conditions such as distance to nearby objects.
Cameras capture visual information, including road markings and traffic signals.
An on-board computer or microprocessor receives and processes the inputs.
Algorithms interpret the situation and determine appropriate actions.
Stored parameters and current readings support decisions.
Actuators operate controls such as brakes, steering and throttle.
The system repeatedly updates its inputs and actions as conditions change.
advice: Keep input, processing and actuator output separate.

adviceSources.comment: Describe the microprocessor comparing data with a preset value and signalling the actuator to apply the brakes. Do not treat the sensor as the microprocessor or replace the requested processing explanation with sensor operation.

Describe sensor-based obstacle detection and transmission of data to the microprocessor. Do not answer only about the microprocessor or assume that the sensor alone completes the whole detection/control process.

answerGroups.text:
Four from:
The microprocessor receives the data
A preset value for the distance is stored in the microprocessor
The microprocessor compares this data to the minimum distance/preset value
If the data is less than the preset value the microprocessor sends a signal to the actuator
The actuator applies the brakes
If the data is more than the preset value the microprocessor does nothing
Process is continuous

Four from:
Data are sent back to the sensor
The sensors scan continually
The sensor captures the reflected data
The sensor captures analogue data
The data from the sensor is sent by the ADC

Ultrasonic sensors use reflected sound, commonly for nearby obstacles.
Several inputs can be combined to build a picture of the surroundings.

It decides whether an action is needed.
It sends control signals to the appropriate actuators.
Actuators can apply the brakes, turn the steering, change gears or adjust the throttle.
For automatic braking, a distance below a preset safe value can trigger braking.
The process repeats continuously as new data arrives.

question: Autonomous car at traffic lights: control sequence
points: Cameras or other inputs detect the traffic signal and surrounding road conditions.
The processor interprets the signal and decides whether to stop.
It sends signals to actuators to reduce speed and apply the brakes.
The vehicle remains stopped while the signal requires it.
The system continues monitoring the signal, pedestrians and other vehicles.
When the signal permits movement and the route is safe, the processor commands movement.
Steering, acceleration and braking continue to be adjusted using fresh sensor data.

question: Autonomous vehicles: cybersecurity and privacy

False or blocked sensor data can cause unsafe decisions.
Communication links and software require protection from tampering.
Location records can reveal the user's movements.
Account or owner information may be exposed if systems are compromised.
Security updates and controlled access help reduce these risks.
A security failure can affect physical safety as well as personal data.

Cameras, including infrared cameras where fitted, provide additional information.

Actuators control acceleration and braking.
Door mechanisms open and close under system control.
Door sensors help prevent unsafe movement when an obstruction is detected.

Navigation systems, including GPS where available, supply position information.

Actuators adjust components such as throttle, wing flaps and rudder.
Reliable handling of abnormal conditions is essential.

title: Health risks: overview
question: Health risks: overview
points: Prolonged IT use can be associated with eyestrain, headaches, RSI and back or neck discomfort.

sectionName: Potential health problems related to the prolonged use of IT equipment
title: Ozone irritation: source and symptoms
question: Ozone irritation: source and symptoms
points: Some laser printing equipment can emit ozone during operation.

The textbook also identifies dry skin as a possible irritation symptom.
This is a health issue associated with emissions, rather than a mechanical printer hazard.
The amount of exposure depends on the equipment and ventilation.
Not every printer produces the same emissions.
advice: Explain the printer-emission health effect accurately rather than confusing it with a physical safety hazard.

adviceSources.comment: Give both similarities and clear differences between a laser printer and plotter. Both produce high-quality hard copy; plotters use ink and do not only draw graphs. Develop comparisons, specify what is printed faster, and explain ozone-related effects accurately.

title: Streaming versus downloading
question: Streaming versus downloading
points: Streaming delivers live or recorded media over a network for playback as data arrives.
The user need not retain a complete downloaded copy before playback begins.
Downloading saves a file locally so it can be used later, subject to access restrictions.

Insufficient bandwidth can cause pauses, lag or sound and picture synchronisation problems.
A downloaded file uses local storage but may be usable without a continuing connection.
Subscriptions, availability and ownership depend on the service; streaming is not necessarily free.
advice: Define streaming as playback of delivered media, use generic terms and develop both benefits and drawbacks in the stated context.

The player takes data from the buffer at the rate needed for playback.

If the buffer empties, playback may pause while more data arrives.
A consistently inadequate connection cannot be fixed by buffering alone.
Some initial delay may be needed to collect enough data to start smoothly.

title: Cellular networks and handover
question: Cellular networks and handover
points: A cellular network divides an area into coverage cells served by base stations.

Overlapping coverage helps maintain communication as the user moves.
As signal conditions change, the network can hand the connection to another cell.
This transfer is called handover.
Coverage depends on the availability of suitable base stations and radio conditions.
Remote areas may have limited cellular coverage.

title: Computer models and simulations
question: Computer models and simulations
points: A computer model is a software representation of a real system.

title: Bottling-plant control sequence
question: Bottling-plant control sequence
points: A sensor detects a bottle in the filling position.
The controller receives the signal and commands an actuator to open the filling valve.

When the bottle is full, an actuator closes the valve.
The controller activates the conveyor motor to move the filled bottle and position the next one.
The cycle repeats until stopped or a fault requires intervention.

title: Cheques: advantages and disadvantages
question: Cheques: advantages and disadvantages
points: A cheque gives written instructions for a bank payment.
It provides a record of the intended payee and amount.
It avoids carrying the equivalent amount in cash.
Processing and clearing can take time.
A cheque can be rejected if it is invalid or funds are insufficient.
Forgery, alteration or theft can create fraud risks.
Acceptance, charges and any stop-payment arrangements depend on banking rules.
Electronic payments can be more convenient where available.

title: Image-based cheque clearing
question: Image-based cheque clearing
points: The cheque is scanned to create a digital image.
Recognition software reads details such as bank information, account information and the amount.
Relevant image and data files are sent electronically through the clearing system.
The paying bank checks the account, cheque validity and payment conditions.
It sends an approval or rejection response.
Approved payments lead to the appropriate account updates.
Image transfer reduces the need to transport the original paper cheque through every stage.
Recognition errors and uncertain details require checking.

title: Patient and pharmacy databases

Scans and other investigation results can be linked to the record.
Authorised staff can search for relevant information quickly.
Shared records support communication between healthcare providers.
Pharmacy records and electronic prescriptions support medication management.
Current records can help staff identify known allergies or possible medicine interactions.
Confidential information needs controlled access and accurate updating.

Clinicians can use the model to explain a condition or planned procedure.
Surgeons can plan and practise aspects of a procedure before operating.
A bone model can help test the position of plates or screws.

title: Expert systems: advantages and disadvantages
question: Expert systems: advantages and disadvantages
points: Expert systems can provide consistent answers to the same facts and rules.
Stored expertise can be available when a human specialist is unavailable.
They can process relevant facts quickly and explain their reasoning.
Knowledge can be retained and shared.
Building and maintaining the system requires expertise, time and money.
Incorrect user input or inaccurate stored knowledge can cause incorrect conclusions.
New situations absent from the knowledge base may not be handled well.
Users can become overdependent on an impersonal system with limited judgement.

title: ANPR: recognition process
question: ANPR: recognition process
points: A camera captures an image of the vehicle.
Software locates the number-plate region.
Brightness and contrast can be adjusted to improve readability.
The characters are separated and recognised using OCR.
The result is converted into machine-readable registration text.
The registration can be stored with the capture time and location.
It can then be compared with relevant database records.
The camera captures the image; software and the database perform the recognition and checking stages.
advice: Include software recognition and database comparison; the camera alone does not perform the whole ANPR process.

adviceSources.question: 8c
adviceSources.comment: Explain the connected computer and database as well as the camera in ANPR. The camera alone does not perform all the intelligent processing. Do not replace the gate-security scenario with road safety.

title: ANPR car-park entry, payment and exit
question: ANPR car-park entry, payment and exit

It records the entry time and booking or ticket information as required.
When payment is requested, the system calculates the charge from the relevant record.
Payment is recorded against the registration or parking session.
At exit, another capture identifies the vehicle.
The system checks payment, authorisation or other exit conditions.
A control signal raises the barrier when the conditions are met.
Unrecognised plates or incomplete payment need an exception process.
advice: Keep the car-park access process in context rather than switching to speeding or stolen-vehicle detection.

title: ANPR uses and advantages
question: ANPR uses and advantages
points: ANPR automates identification of vehicle registrations.
A car park can admit only registrations in its authorised database.
Automatic checking can reduce manual work and staff costs.
Entry and exit records support parking charges and traffic analysis.
Time-stamped observations can support average-speed calculations over a known distance.
Registrations can be checked for congestion charging or vehicles of interest.
The benefit depends on the particular system and its database.
Security and privacy need to be considered alongside convenience.
advice: Explain benefits for the stated ANPR use; school parking and road-speed monitoring are different contexts.

title: ANPR limitations
question: ANPR limitations
points: Dirt or damage can make plate characters difficult to recognise.
Another vehicle or person can obstruct the camera's view.
Poor lighting, weather or camera position can reduce image quality.
Unusual fonts or character spacing can cause misreading.
A valid plate absent from the database may be rejected.
Cloned plates can cause the wrong vehicle to appear authorised.
Records of movements raise privacy and access-control concerns.
Database maintenance and correction of recognition errors are necessary.
advice: Link the condition to its effect on recognition, such as dirt obscuring characters, rather than naming a bare problem.

adviceSources.question: 8d

title: RFID advantages and disadvantages
question: RFID advantages and disadvantages
points: RFID uses radio waves to identify tags.
A tag can be read without direct optical line of sight.
Suitable systems can read several tags in one operation.
Tags can remain readable when the visible surface is defaced, if the electronics are intact.
Some tags hold more data and support rewriting.
Automation can speed identification and tracking.
Tags and readers can cost more than printed barcodes.
Interference, collisions or deliberate jamming can affect reading.
Data may be intercepted if the system lacks appropriate protection.
advice: RFID still requires reading. Explain radio-based identification without line of sight rather than claiming no scanning is needed.

adviceSources.question: 7a

title: RFID tags: components and power
question: RFID tags: components and power
points: An RFID tag contains a chip and an antenna.
The chip stores identifying data or other information.
A reader transmits radio signals and receives the tag's response.
A passive tag obtains the energy needed for its response from the reader's field.
An active tag has its own power source, usually a battery.
Read distance and capabilities depend on the tag and system.
The returned identifier can be used to find further details in a database.
advice: Name the RFID reader and explain reader activation followed by the tag’s returned data. RFID alone names the technology.

question: RFID passports

The chip stores relevant identity and biometric information.
A compatible reader communicates with the chip at a checkpoint.

Access controls and cryptographic checks help protect the stored information and authenticity.

The payment system checks and processes the transaction.
A PIN or other check may be required according to the transaction rules.
Contactless communication is the input method; authorisation still takes place through the payment process.

title: NFC versus general RFID
question: NFC versus general RFID
points: NFC is a short-range contactless technology related to RFID.
It operates over close proximity, typically a few centimetres.
General RFID systems can have different operating frequencies and ranges.
NFC devices can act as readers or emulate compatible cards.
A connection can be initiated by bringing compatible devices close together.
Ordinary NFC exchanges do not require Bluetooth-style pairing.
Close proximity is useful for deliberate tap interactions but does not by itself guarantee security.

title: NFC modes
question: NFC modes
points: In reader/writer mode, an NFC device reads data from or writes data to a compatible tag.
A phone can read a tag containing a link or other information.
In card-emulation mode, a device behaves like a contactless card.
Card emulation can support payment, access or transport-ticket interactions.
In peer-to-peer mode, two compatible NFC devices exchange information.
The roles and supported functions depend on the devices and application.
Reader/writer mode is not limited to a passive tablet receiving one-way advertisements.
textbookScope: Peer-to-peer, read/write and card emulation; sharing, tags, payments and transport access. Textbook role descriptions need checking before answer cards.

title: Biometric recognition categories
question: Biometric recognition categories
points: Biometric recognition identifies or authenticates people using measurable characteristics.
Physical examples include fingerprints, hand geometry, face, iris and retina patterns.
Voice characteristics and some behavioural patterns can also be used.
Captured features are compared with enrolled templates.
Biometrics are difficult to forget or lend in the same way as a card or password.
Enrolment, equipment, recognition errors and privacy are possible limitations.
Name the biometric method rather than only its capture device.
Keep the selected method consistent with the scenario.

title: GPS/GNSS positioning
question: GPS/GNSS positioning
points: GNSS means Global Navigation Satellite System; GPS is one such system.
Satellites broadcast signals containing precise timing and orbital-position information.
A receiver measures signal travel times to estimate its distance from satellites.
Using several satellites, the receiver calculates its position.
A normal three-dimensional fix also needs correction of the receiver's clock, usually using at least four satellites.
The GPS receiver receives broadcast signals; it need not send a request to the satellites.
GPS supplies position and time, while route planning requires additional maps and software.
advice: Satellites broadcast position and timing signals; the receiver calculates its location without sending a request back to them.

adviceSources.question: 3b
adviceSources.comment: Explain satellite navigation accurately: satellites broadcast signals towards Earth and the vehicle’s satnav interprets them. Do not claim that the vehicle sends a signal to a satellite or that a satellite targets the vehicle directly.

title: Satellite navigation
question: Satellite navigation
points: A satellite-navigation device receives satellite signals and calculates its position.
The position is placed on a stored digital map.
The user enters a destination and relevant route preferences.
An algorithm calculates a route using the map and permitted roads.
The device displays directions and can provide spoken instructions.
Its position is updated as the user moves.
A route can be recalculated if the user leaves it or new traffic information is available.
Traffic updates require an additional information source; GPS signals do not contain every road condition.
advice: Distinguish GPS positioning, satnav routing and GIS analysis. Do not claim that the vehicle sends a navigation request to a satellite.

title: Validation: purpose and limits
question: Validation: purpose and limits
points: Validation is an automatic check that input meets specified acceptance criteria.
It tests whether data is sensible, reasonable or in the required form.
Examples include range, type, length, format, presence and check-digit checks.

Verification checks accurate copying from the source rather than acceptability.

advice: Validation checks acceptance criteria; verification checks accurate copying. Neither proves the original source is correct, and verification here is not identity checking.

adviceSources.comment: Validation checks whether data is reasonable and meets set criteria. Verification checks whether it was copied correctly; the source itself may be wrong. Both reduce errors but do not eliminate them. Verification here does not mean confirming someone’s identity.

title: Presence check
question: Presence check
points: A presence check tests that a required field has not been left empty.
It rejects a null or missing entry where a value is mandatory.

For example, a sale date may legitimately be empty before an item is sold.
Presence does not prove that an entered value is correct, well formed or within range.
advice: Check whether the field is mandatory. A field that can legitimately be empty does not need a presence check.

title: Check digit
question: Check digit
points: A check digit is an additional digit calculated from the other digits in an identifier.
The calculation follows a defined algorithm.
On entry or reading, the system repeats the calculation and checks the result.
A mismatch indicates that the code may have been entered or read incorrectly.
Depending on the algorithm, it can detect substitutions, transpositions or missing or extra digits.
It detects some errors but does not itself correct the original data.
Not every possible error is detected by every check-digit method.
advice: Explain the calculated extra digit in the context of the identifier rather than giving only a generic validation label.

title: Double-entry verification
question: Double-entry verification
points: Double-entry verification requires the same source data to be entered independently twice.
The two entries can be made by one person on separate attempts or by different people.
The computer compares the entries.
A mismatch is flagged for checking against the source.
Visual verification instead involves a person comparing entered data directly with the original.
Both aim to detect copying errors.
Matching entries do not prove that the original source is correct.
Data verification here is different from authenticating a person's identity.
advice: Include independent second entry and computer comparison. Visual verification compares with the source; neither proves the source itself is correct.

adviceSources.question: 10a
adviceSources.comment: Compare both verification methods using the original source and accurate copying. Verification does not guarantee that the original data is correct. Develop double entry beyond “entered twice”, including separate entry and computer comparison. Visual verification uses a source document; proofreading need not.

title: Electrocution: causes and prevention
question: Electrocution: causes and prevention
points: Liquids spilling onto electrical equipment can create a risk of electric shock.
Exposed conductors, damaged insulation and unsafe plugs or sockets can also cause injury.
Keep drinks and other liquids away from computer equipment.
Inspect accessible cables and stop using equipment with visible damage.
Qualified personnel should carry out appropriate electrical checks and repairs.
Suitable residual-current protection can reduce the risk of serious electric shock.
Do not handle exposed live wiring or attempt electrical repairs as an ordinary user.
advice: Link the precaution to the equipment: keep liquids away from electrical devices. The risk to the person is electric shock, not just a broken computer.

title: Fire: causes and prevention
question: Fire: causes and prevention
points: Overloaded sockets or extension blocks can overheat.
Blocked cooling vents and accumulated dust can cause equipment to overheat.
Damaged wiring can cause a short circuit and fire.
Avoid overloading power outlets and use an appropriate electrical installation.
Keep ventilation openings unobstructed.
Arrange suitable inspection, cleaning and maintenance of equipment.

title: Worms versus viruses

A virus replicates through an infected host file or program.
Both can consume resources and disrupt operation.

title: Fingerprint advantages and disadvantages

points: A user does not have to remember a password or carry a separate identity card.

Fingerprints provide distinguishing features for identification.
Enrolment and suitable capture equipment have costs.
Dirty, wet or injured fingers can cause failed recognition.
Stored biometric information raises privacy and security concerns.
The system needs a suitable way to handle a genuine user who cannot be recognised.

title: Digital certificates and certificate authorities
question: Digital certificates and certificate authorities
points: A digital certificate binds identity information, such as a website's domain, to a public key.
It is digitally signed by an issuer such as a certificate authority.
It contains the subject's identifying details and public key.
Other contents include issuer information, serial number and validity dates.
The browser checks the certificate and its chain against trusted issuers.
It checks that the certificate is valid for the intended site.
The certificate contains a public key, not the holder's private key.
A valid connection certificate does not guarantee that every request or item of website content is trustworthy.
advice: Specify certificate contents precisely, such as the subject or owner’s name and public key. Relate its purpose to the website’s identity.

title: User IDs and passwords
question: User IDs and passwords
points: A user ID identifies the account being accessed.
A password is a secret used to authenticate access to that account.
The system checks the submitted credentials.
The user receives the access rights assigned to the account.
Account identifiers support monitoring of account activity.
Password masking reduces casual observation of the displayed entry.
Repeated failed attempts may cause a lockout or another protective response.

title: Strong versus weak passwords
question: Strong versus weak passwords
points: A strong password or passphrase is long and difficult to guess.
Avoid personal details, common predictable choices and obvious keyboard sequences.
Character variety can make a chosen password harder to guess, but length and unpredictability are important.
Use a distinct password for each account to limit the effect of one compromise.
A memorable but unpredictable phrase can be easier to manage than a short complicated pattern.
Do not share credentials or expose them to observation.
A strong password does not stop phishing, keylogging or every form of interception.
Extra authentication can reduce dependence on the password alone.
advice: Give distinct strength rules and justify unpredictability rather than choosing a password only because it is memorable.

adviceSources.question: 3a
adviceSources.comment: Choose the most appropriate secure password and justify its strength. Do not choose solely because it is easy to remember. Correct reasons could receive follow-on marks even after an incorrect choice.

title: Password protection, verification and reset
question: Password protection, verification and reset
points: Keep account credentials secret and use appropriate protection against spyware or keylogging.
Mask password entry when other people can observe the screen.
Entering a new password twice can detect a typing mismatch during setup.
Attempt limits or temporary lockout reduce repeated online guessing.
A reset process verifies the request and provides a controlled way to set a replacement.
Check reset messages independently if they are unexpected.
Change passwords when compromised or when required by an appropriate account-recovery process.
Frequent compulsory changes can lead to predictable variants or forgotten passwords.
Masking, double-entry verification and authentication serve different purposes.
advice: Match the safeguard to the threat: protecting against keylogging differs from preventing observation or reducing password guessing.

adviceSources.question: 12b
adviceSources.comment: Address the malware-based interception involved in keylogging. Strong passwords or covering the keyboard do not prevent this threat.

title: Software copyright and infringement
question: Software copyright and infringement
points: Copyright protects intellectual work and gives the rights holder control over specified uses such as copying.
The owner can grant permission through a licence.
Unauthorised copying, distribution or reuse of protected software can infringe those rights.
Permission may be required before copying code or including protected material in another product.
Acknowledge sources where required, but a credit alone does not automatically replace permission.
Copyright helps recognise creators, protect their work and discourage plagiarism.
Copyright concerns intellectual work; data protection concerns appropriate handling of personal data.
The permitted uses depend on the licence and applicable rules.
advice: Explain rights over intellectual work and permission to copy. Copyright is not data protection and does not prohibit every authorised copy.

adviceSources.question: 12b
adviceSources.comment: Explain copyright accurately. It does not simply prevent all copying of data; many candidates misunderstood this purpose.

title: Network and multiple-computer licences
question: Network and multiple-computer licences
points: A licence defines the permitted use of software.
A single-computer or single-user licence does not automatically permit unrestricted use across a network.
A suitable multiple-computer or network licence allows use within its stated conditions.
Conditions can limit installations, users or simultaneous access.
Organisations need permission covering the way the software is deployed.
The licence must be checked rather than assuming that possession of one copy permits every installation.

title: Product keys
question: Product keys
points: A product key is a supplied code used to support authorised installation or activation.
It may contain letters and numbers.
The user enters the code when the software requires it.
The program or an online service checks whether the key is valid.
Activation rules can limit unauthorised installations or use.
Online account checks can also enforce permitted access or concurrent-use limits.
A product key is different from an ordinary account password or an anti-virus tool.

The user may need to accept the agreement before installation or use continues.

Accepting an agreement does not grant rights beyond those stated.
Licence conditions are a rights-management measure rather than a method of scanning for malware.
advice: Describe the agreement between vendor and user about permitted software use, not a malware-protection process.

question: Original-media checks
points: Some software checks that its required original CD, DVD or memory device is present.
The program refuses to run if the required medium is absent.

It is a software-protection approach, not simply supplying the program on a disc.

question: Software-protection dongles
points: A software-protection dongle is a hardware device connected to the computer, often through USB.
It supplies required authorisation information or functionality.
The program checks for the dongle.
Without the required valid dongle, the software will not run or unlock its protected functions.
It discourages use of copied software without the authorised hardware.
The word dongle can also describe devices such as wireless adapters; that is a different use of the term.

title: Anti-piracy organisations and penalties
question: Anti-piracy organisations and penalties
points: Software-industry and intellectual-property organisations can support efforts against unauthorised software distribution.
The textbook gives FAST, IIPA and JIPA as examples in its historical discussion.
Their activities can include awareness, representation or support for rights enforcement, depending on the organisation.
Rights holders can pursue infringements through the applicable legal processes.
Possible consequences can include an order to stop unauthorised use or financial penalties.
A historical case illustrates enforcement but does not establish a universal current penalty.
Organisational roles and legal consequences depend on the place, time and circumstances.

title: Email legislation and consent
question: Email legislation and consent
points: Email laws and consent rules aim to reduce misuse of electronic communication.

Recipients should have an appropriate way to opt out or unsubscribe.
Sender information and subject lines should not be false or misleading.
Organisations should explain how subscribers' personal information is used.
Collecting addresses without proper permission can breach applicable rules.
The exact obligations depend on the jurisdiction and type of message.
Mailing-list administrators need to maintain consent and membership records.

title: Email copyright and confidentiality
question: Email copyright and confidentiality
points: An email or attachment can contain copyright-protected or confidential material.
Receiving a message does not automatically give unrestricted permission to copy or redistribute its contents.
Check the relevant permissions, licence terms and organisational policy before forwarding.
Check the intended recipients and any confidentiality instructions.
Share only information the new recipients are authorised to receive.

advice: Check the exact recipient and intended attachment, remove unnecessary personal information and protect confidential content.

title: Passive versus active email attacks
question: Passive versus active email attacks
points: A passive attack observes or discloses information without changing the communication being observed.
Unauthorised reading of a message can breach confidentiality.
An active attack changes data or disrupts communication or service.
Examples include modifying a message or overwhelming a service with traffic.
Malicious messages can attempt to infect or deceive the recipient.
Encryption protects confidentiality, while other controls are needed for integrity, access and service availability.
Classify an attack by what it does rather than assuming every attack has the same effect.
textbookScope: Unauthorised disclosure versus modification, denial of service and malicious messages.

title: To, Cc and Bcc

title: Objectivity, currency and completeness
question: Objectivity, currency and completeness
points: Check when the information was published and last reviewed.
Consider whether it is current enough for the question being researched.
Identify commercial, political or other interests that may influence the account.
Separate evidence from opinion, advertising and unsupported claims.
Check whether competing arguments and relevant limitations are included.
Look for references supporting important statements.
Repeated identical or uniformly positive reviews can be a warning sign.
A source can be useful while still needing corroboration.
advice: Develop reliability checks such as review dates, independent comparisons and potentially fake reviews.

title: Website legitimacy and working links
question: Website legitimacy and working links
points: Check that the site represents the organisation it claims to represent.
Review its authorship, contact information, evidence and relevant external references.
Working links and maintained pages can indicate active upkeep.
Broken links or abandoned pages can suggest outdated material.
A convincing layout is not proof that the publisher is genuine.
HTTPS protects the connection but does not establish the truth of the content.
Compare important claims with reputable independent sources.
Assess several signals together rather than relying on one appearance feature.
advice: Assess source reliability through evidence and corroboration; do not substitute the advertised product’s features.

title: Protocols and HTTP
question: Protocols and HTTP
points: A protocol is an agreed set of rules for communication between systems.
HTTP stands for Hypertext Transfer Protocol.
A client sends a request for a web resource.
A server returns a response, such as page data or an error status.
Browsers use the supplied resources to display web content.
HTTP without transport encryption does not protect the content against network eavesdropping.
HTTPS uses HTTP over a protected TLS connection.

title: HTTPS and SSL
question: HTTPS and SSL
points: HTTPS is HTTP over an encrypted and authenticated TLS connection.
The textbook's SSL terminology refers to the predecessor of modern TLS.
Encryption protects data in transit between the browser and server.
Integrity checks help detect tampering.
A server certificate supports verification of the requested site's identity.
The address uses https, while browser connection indicators depend on the browser.
An encrypted connection does not guarantee that the website's claims or requests are honest.
Do not assume every browser defaults to unencrypted HTTP when a scheme is omitted.
advice: Explain the encrypted browser-to-server link and its protection. Expanding SSL or saying extra security alone is insufficient.

title: File transfer protocol (FTP)
question: File transfer protocol (FTP)
points: FTP stands for File Transfer Protocol.
It is used to transfer files between a client and server.
It supports uploading and downloading according to access permissions.
A suitable client connects to the server and provides any required credentials.
Ordinary FTP does not itself encrypt the transferred data or credentials.
FTPS adds TLS to FTP.
SFTP is a different secure file-transfer protocol operating over SSH.
Use a compatible transfer client rather than assuming every web browser supports FTP addresses.
advice: Name actual secure-transfer protocols rather than devices or general security procedures.

title: Secure connections: uses
question: Secure connections: uses
points: Protected connections support online banking, shopping and other confidential transactions.
Suitable encrypted protocols protect email transport and file transfer.
Cloud, intranet and extranet services can use protected access.
Calls and messaging can also use appropriate encryption.
The purpose is to reduce disclosure or undetected modification during transmission.
Authentication helps establish the party or endpoint being contacted.
Stored copies and the devices at each endpoint need their own protection.
Using cloud storage or sending a password does not automatically make every transfer secure.
advice: Explain how encryption protects transferred information rather than merely naming another security measure.

title: Arguments for internet control
question: Arguments for internet control
points: Supporters of internet controls argue that they can reduce access to illegal or harmful material.
Controls can help protect children and other vulnerable users.
Moderation can reduce abuse and the distribution of inappropriate content.
Intervention can limit some fraudulent or misleading information.
Clear rules and enforcement can support accountability.
Effectiveness depends on the scope, implementation and reliability of the controls.
Control does not guarantee that every harmful item will be prevented.

title: Arguments against internet control
question: Arguments against internet control
points: Monitoring and enforcement across many sites can be expensive.
Different jurisdictions and global distribution make rules difficult to apply consistently.
Overbroad restrictions can limit legitimate expression or access to information.
Judgements about offensive content can be subjective.
Some harmful activity is already covered by existing rules.
Material may remain available through other routes.
Decision-making and appeal arrangements matter when legitimate content can be blocked.
Arguments should weigh protection against cost, practicality and rights.
textbookScope: Cost, global enforcement, free expression, existing laws, subjective judgements and alternative information sources.

title: Filtering and education
question: Filtering and education
points: Content filters can restrict access to selected sites or categories.
Allow lists and deny lists can be configured on suitable services, routers or devices.
Parental controls can set access times and other restrictions.
Providers may offer filtering services for home or mobile connections.
Monitoring history observes use; blocking or time limits control it.
Filters can miss harmful content or block useful material.
Education helps users recognise risks, verify sources and respond appropriately.
Trusted adult or teacher guidance complements technical controls.
Restrictions should be suitable for the intended users and purpose.
advice: Distinguish monitoring activity from restricting access through blocked sites, filters or time limits.
